Biography

Introduction: The Heartbeat of the Grenadines

In the maritime world of the Caribbean, the island of Carriacou and Petite Martinique holds a distinct, almost mythological status. It is a place where traditional wooden sloops are still built by hand on the beach, and where the rhythmic pounding of the sea is matched only by the beating of the ancestral drum. At the center of this cultural nexus stood Ferguson "Sugar" Adams (c. 1890–1983), a legendary master of the Big Drum (also known as the Nation Dance). While the master shipwrights of the island shaped the physical vessels that navigated the inter-island trading routes, it was Sugar Adams who gave these ships their soul.

Though not a shipwright himself, Adams was the spiritual anchor of Carriacou's boatbuilding heritage. In the villages of Windward and L'Esterre, no vessel was deemed seaworthy until it had been properly blessed through the rituals of the Big Drum. As the preeminent "cut" drummer of the 20th century, Adams commanded the ceremonies that married Carriacou’s Scottish maritime techniques with its profound African spiritual traditions, ensuring that the legacy of the island remained unbroken for generations.

Early Life and the African Roots of Carriacou

Born in the late 19th century on the island of Carriacou—a small dependency of Grenada—Ferguson Adams grew up in a society deeply defined by isolation and historical retention. Following the abolition of slavery and the subsequent decline of the sugar and cotton plantations, many of the Scottish and English landowners abandoned the island. The formerly enslaved African population, left to govern their own social and cultural lives, fiercely preserved their heritage. Because Carriacou was small and somewhat neglected by colonial authorities, the African nations from which the population originated—Kromanti, Igbo, Manding, Arada, and Temne—maintained their distinct identities.

From a young age, Adams was immersed in the "Nation Dance" or Big Drum tradition. This ceremonial music was not merely entertainment; it was a sacred liturgy used to honor the "Old Parents" (ancestors), seek blessings for the harvest, heal the sick, and launch ships. The instrumentation consisted of three drums, typically crafted from small rum kegs inherited from the island’s inter-island smuggling and trading networks. The kegs were tightly bound with goatskin (the lapo-kabwit). Two smaller "boula" drums provided a steady, foundational rhythm, while the larger "cut" drum (or cot) was used for complex improvisation, dictating the movements of the dancers.

Sugar Adams displayed an extraordinary, almost preternatural affinity for the cut drum. To master this instrument required not only immense physical stamina and technical dexterity but also an encyclopedic knowledge of the specific rhythms, chants, and linguistic fragments associated with each African nation. Adams became a living archive of these rhythms, memorizing the subtle polyrhythmic shifts that distinguished a Kromanti war dance from an Igbo social dance.

The Boatbuilding Heritage of Windward

To understand the vital importance of Sugar Adams’s role, one must understand the economic and cultural lifeblood of Carriacou: boatbuilding. In the eastern village of Windward, descendants of Scottish shipwrights and African craftsmen blended their skills to create the legendary Carriacou sloop. Built entirely by eye and oral tradition, without the use of blueprints, these wooden sailing vessels were constructed on the open beach under the shade of manchineel trees.

These boats were essential for survival. They formed the backbone of the inter-island trading network stretching from Trinidad to Martinique, carrying provisions, livestock, smuggled goods, and the famous "Jack Iron" overproof rum. But in the minds of the Carriacouans, a boat was not merely a construction of white cedar and pitch pine. It was a living entity that would face the wrath of the sea, the unpredictable trade winds, and the treacherous currents of the Kick 'em Jenny submarine volcano.

Therefore, a ship could not simply be pushed into the water. It required a baptism. It required the Big Drum.

"The shipwright shapes the timber with adze and saw, but it is the master drummer who breathes life into the vessel. Without the rhythm of the Big Drum, the sloop has no spirit to navigate the treacherous currents of the Grenadines."

The Sacred Launching Ceremony

The boat launching ceremonies of Carriacou are massive, multi-day community festivals, and during his prime, Sugar Adams was the undisputed master of ceremonies. When a prominent shipwright like Zephaniah McLaren or a member of the Enoe family finished a vessel, Adams and his troupe of drummers and chantwells (lead singers, often elderly women who knew the ancestral songs) would be summoned to the shoreline.

The ritual began with the "Saraca"—a sacrificial feast. A sheep or goat would be slaughtered, and its blood, mixed with holy water and Jack Iron rum, was sprinkled over the bow of the new ship to appease the ancestors and bless the vessel. "Parents' Plates" filled with unseasoned food were laid out for the spirits.

Then, Adams would take his place at the cut drum. Straddling the wooden keg, he would strike the goatskin with his bare hands, calling the community to order. The drumming would begin with the solemn, majestic Kromanti rhythms—the music of the ancestors. As Adams played, he entered a state of deep spiritual flow, his hands moving in a blur as the rhythm resonated through the humid Caribbean air and bounced off the wooden hull of the new sloop.

As the time for the launch approached, the tempo would increase. Hundreds of villagers would line up along heavy ropes attached to the ship, waiting to pull the massive vessel over wooden rollers into the sea. Adams’s drumming served as the metronome for this grueling physical labor. He played the "Juba" and the "Hallecord," rhythms designed to synchronize the pulling and inject the workers with adrenaline. When the boat finally crested the sand and splashed into the turquoise waters of the Caribbean Sea, the drumming would reach a triumphant, feverish climax, followed by days of dancing, drinking, and celebration.

Documenting the Master: Alan Lomax and Global Recognition

For decades, Adams performed these duties in relative obscurity, known only to the people of the Grenadines. However, in the mid-20th century, ethnomusicologists and anthropologists began to recognize the incredible historical value of Carriacou's well-preserved African traditions.

In 1962, the legendary American folklorist Alan Lomax traveled to Carriacou with a heavy reel-to-reel tape recorder. Lomax was astounded by what he found: a community that had retained the music of West Africa more faithfully than almost anywhere else in the Americas. At the center of Lomax's recordings was Sugar Adams. Lomax captured Adams's masterful playing on the cut drum, documenting the intricate rhythms of the Nation Dance for the Library of Congress and international archives.

These recordings brought Adams international acclaim. He was recognized as one of the most important traditional musicians in the Caribbean. In 1966, when Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip visited the region, Sugar Adams and his troupe were chosen to perform the Big Drum for the royal couple, showcasing the pride and heritage of Carriacou on a global stage.

"To hear Sugar Adams play the 'cut' drum was to hear the voices of the ancestors calling out across the Middle Passage, ensuring that no Carriacouan would ever forget their Nation."

Legacy and Passing the Torch

As Adams grew older, he became acutely aware of the need to pass on his knowledge. The modern world was encroaching on Carriacou; radios, outboard motors, and migration threatened to erode the old ways. Adams took on apprentices, most notably Winston Fleary, who would go on to become a tireless cultural ambassador for Carriacou, bringing the Big Drum to audiences in North America and Europe.

Ferguson "Sugar" Adams passed away in 1983, leaving behind an island forever shaped by his hands. Today, the tradition of traditional wooden boatbuilding continues in Carriacou, celebrated annually at the Carriacou Regatta. And while modern tools have made their way into the shipyards, the launching of a vessel remains a sacred act. When a new sloop rolls down the beach at Windward and splashes into the sea, it does so to the rhythm of the Big Drum—a rhythm that Sugar Adams protected, perfected, and passed into eternity.

Major Contributions

  • Ferguson "Sugar" Adams was the preeminent master of the Carriacou Big Drum (Nation Dance), an ancient musical and spiritual tradition that traces its roots directly back to West African nations.
  • His unparalleled skill on the "cut" drum preserved the intricate polyrhythms of the Kromanti, Igbo, and Manding nations.
  • Adams's leadership in the Big Drum troupes ensured that this unique cultural artifact survived the pressures of modernity and colonialism, eventually bringing it to the global stage through historic 1962 recordings by ethnomusicologist Alan Lomax and performances for visiting British royalty.
  • Furthermore, Adams served as the spiritual anchor for Carriacou's legendary wooden boatbuilding industry.
  • By commanding the musical rituals at traditional boat launchings on the shores of Windward and L'Esterre, he provided the ceremonial blessings deemed essential for the maritime success of the island's famous sloops.
  • His cultural stewardship solidified the symbiotic relationship between Carriacou's African spiritual heritage and its Scottish-influenced maritime traditions, leaving a legacy that is still celebrated in the Grenadines today.
